channel.title: Concepts :: Go Kure
channel.description: Understand the ideas behind Kure’s design. Architecture - System architecture and component overview Domain Model - The Cluster, Node, Bundle, Application hierarchy Builder Contract - Building an object, when sugar exists, reading the maturity table Design Philosophy - The upstream type over templating, GitOps-native output Package Status - What is supported, limited, consumer-provided, not implemented or only proposed Layout and Flux Naming - How directories, files and Flux objects are named OCI Artifact Layout - How manifests are packaged as OCI artifacts How the kure and launcher models relate kure and go-kure/launcher are two projects with two models, and both use the word Application for something different.

item.title: Domain Model
item.description: Kure models Kubernetes infrastructure as a four-level hierarchy. Each level maps to a concept in GitOps deployment workflows. The Hierarchy Cluster └── Node (tree structure) └── Bundle (deployment unit) └── Application (workload) Cluster The root of the hierarchy, representing a target Kubernetes cluster. A cluster has a name, a tree of nodes, and GitOps configuration specifying which workflow engine to use (Flux or ArgoCD). That configuration can also carry a bootstrap: how Flux itself is installed (in gotk mode, from the flux2 release Kure vendors unless FluxVersion names another) and which source it syncs from, including how an OCI sync source reaches its registry in either mode (SourceSecretRef, SourceProvider, SourceInsecure), whether it verifies the artifact’s signature (SourceVerify), a semver range for its tag (SourceSemVer) and the name of the bootstrap source and Kustomization in either mode (BootstrapConfig.SyncName). In flux-operator mode, the default, BootstrapConfig.FluxVersion and Registry are both required: they become the FluxInstance distribution, an empty value is an error, and no default is filled in. BootstrapConfig.ImagePullSecret names the Secret the Flux controller images are pulled with, in both modes: the gotk install option, or the FluxInstance distribution’s imagePullSecret. It is not a credential for the sync source, and in flux-operator mode neither it nor Registry reaches the flux-operator Deployment in the vendored install bundle. A set BootstrapConfig.Prune reaches the bootstrap Kustomization in both modes, in flux-operator mode as a patch on the operator’s sync Kustomization. Unset keeps each mode’s default: prune: false in gotk mode, the operator’s prune: true in flux-operator mode (go-kure/kure#1088). BootstrapConfig.Labels puts the consumer’s labels on the bootstrap source and Kustomization in both modes, and refuses the keys a Flux controller stamps on them (go-kure/kure#1180).

item.title: Builder Contract
item.description: kure’s Kubernetes foundation is deliberately thin: it hands you the upstream Go struct with its identity filled in, and stops. This page is the consumer’s view of what that means in practice — how to build an object, when a kure helper exists and when there is none, how to read the generated maturity table, and why the layers above the foundation state their opinions as names you can grep for.

item.title: Design Philosophy
item.description: Kure is built on a few core principles that guide its design and API choices. The Upstream Type Over Templating Traditional Kubernetes tooling relies on string-based templating (Helm, Kustomize overlays, Jsonnet). This creates a class of errors that only surface at deploy time — typos in YAML paths, type mismatches, missing fields. Kure uses Go’s type system instead. The type it uses is the upstream one: a Flux Kustomization is kustomizev1.Kustomization, not a kure struct that resembles it.

item.title: Architecture
item.description: Executive Summary Kure is a GitOps domain model and layout engine on a thin Kubernetes foundation. The domain model (pkg/stack) says what a cluster contains; the layout engine (pkg/stack/layout, pkg/stack/fluxcd) writes that out as a reconcilable directory tree of plain YAML; the Kubernetes foundation (pkg/kubernetes) supplies the scheme, one generic constructor, the generated per-kind wrappers over it, and a small admissible set of sugar helpers. The foundation is thin on purpose. The upstream Go struct is the construction API — kure sets identity and stops — so the library’s surface stays small enough to keep stable while the domain model above it carries the opinions.

item.title: Layout and Flux Naming
item.description: This page records how kure names, places and wires the directories and Flux objects it generates from the stack model, and what each change made of it. Part 1 is the behaviour of v0.2.0-beta.15, confirmed by rendering small clusters to disk and to tar. Part 2 is the record of the changes made since, one section per change, each tracked by an issue; every section is marked Shipped. kure, its consumers and their output are pre-release: names, paths and output may change, and live-cluster upgrade effects are not a constraint.

item.title: Package Status
item.description: What each part of kure does today, what it leaves to you, and what is not built. The rows describe the code at the revision the page was built from. Words used on this site Word Meaning Development Built from the latest commit on main. The notice at the top of every page of the development site names the source commit. Published prerelease A tagged release candidate or beta. There is no stable release yet, so every API can still change. Current supported behavior What the code at the built revision does. A row below says Supported only for that. Proposed A design that was written down and not built. Its own file says “proposed, not shipped”, and its Go names do not resolve against pkg/.
